ShapleyForest on Real Data: World Development Indicators

Author

Timothy Shen

Published

July 7, 2026

1 Introduction

This vignette demonstrates the full Shapley Forest (SF) workflow on the World Development Indicators (WDI) dataset from the World Bank. Unlike the gene-expression panels used in the other vignettes, this is a non-biological, genuinely high-dimensional (\(p > n\)) tabular dataset whose features are intuitive to a general audience — GDP per capita, literacy rate, CO₂ emissions, urban population share, and hundreds of other national statistics. The task is to predict a country’s life expectancy at birth from its development profile.

The dataset is deliberately in the same regime as genomics: 544 indicators for only 180 countries. Many indicators are strongly correlated (a country rich on one economic axis tends to be rich on many), so — exactly as with co-expressed genes — a model can “explain” the outcome with almost any one of a redundant block as a stand-in for the others. SF’s screening + shadow-stability machinery exists to cut through blocks like this.

The vignette is separated in four stages:

  1. Data loading and summary
  2. WGCNA
  3. Single SF run and output for exploration purposes
  4. Nested cross-validation comparing all six SF variants with joint hyperparameter tuning

2 Data

We first load the data (included in the package).

if (!require("devtools", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("devtools")
library(devtools)
devtools::install_github("timothyzshen/shapleyforest")

library(shapleyforest)
library(WGCNA)
data(wdi)

wdi_X      <- as.data.frame(wdi$X)
wdi_y      <- wdi$y
wdi_labels <- wdi$labels   # indicator code -> human-readable name

cat("Countries :", nrow(wdi_X), "\n")
Countries : 180 
cat("Indicators:", ncol(wdi_X), "\n")
Indicators: 544 
cat("Outcome   : life expectancy at birth,",
    paste(round(range(wdi_y), 1), collapse = " - "), "years\n")
Outcome   : life expectancy at birth, 50.6 - 85.5 years

We have a \(180 \times 544\) matrix — more features than observations — where the outcome is a continuous quantity (years of life expectancy). This is a regression problem, so throughout we score models by out-of-sample \(R^2\) (and RMSE in years) rather than the AUC used in the classification vignettes.

2.1 Feature correlation structure

Before fitting anything it is worth seeing why this is a hard selection problem: most of these indicators move together. Rather than an unreadable \(544 \times 544\) heatmap, we summarise the redundancy directly — the distribution of absolute pairwise Spearman (rank) correlations among all indicators. We use Spearman rather than Pearson because development indicators are heavily skewed (GDP, population, and land area span orders of magnitude) and often related monotonically but non-linearly; a rank correlation captures those associations that raw Pearson understates.

library(ggplot2)

cor_mat <- cor(wdi_X, method = "spearman")
off_diag <- abs(cor_mat[upper.tri(cor_mat)])

ggplot(data.frame(r = off_diag), aes(x = r)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1F77B4", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", colour = "tomato") +
  labs(title    = "Pairwise redundancy among indicators",
       subtitle = sprintf("%.1f%% of pairs have |rho| > 0.7",
                          100 * mean(off_diag > 0.7)),
       x = "Absolute Spearman correlation", y = "Number of indicator pairs") +
  theme_bw()

3 WGCNA Module Detection

Before running SF we perform WGCNA ourselves to build the network structure. sf() can run WGCNA internally, but doing it manually lets us select the parameters and inspect the modules before handing them off.

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
enableWGCNAThreads()
Allowing parallel execution with up to 7 working processes.

3.1 Rank-transform for the network

WGCNA builds its network from pairwise correlations, so it inherits Pearson’s weakness on skewed, non-linearly-related data. On the raw indicators this is severe: a Pearson-based network leaves ~80% of indicators unassigned, not because they lack structure but because their monotonic associations do not show up as high linear correlations. We therefore rank-transform every indicator before building the network — equivalent to using Spearman correlations — which recovers a rich, well-populated module structure. This transform is used only to define modules; SF itself is fit on the raw indicators (random forests are invariant to monotonic transforms, so this changes the module labels, not the model).

wdi_Xnet <- as.data.frame(lapply(wdi_X, rank))
rownames(wdi_Xnet) <- rownames(wdi_X)

3.2 Soft-threshold power selection

WGCNA constructs a weighted co-expression-style network by raising pairwise correlations to a soft-thresholding power \(\beta\). The chosen power should make the resulting network approximately scale-free (\(R^2 \geq 0.8\)) while keeping mean connectivity reasonably high. We use a signed network — the World Bank authors’ recommended default for real data — so that positively- and negatively-associated indicators land in different modules.

powers <- c(1:10, seq(12, 20, by = 2))

sft <- pickSoftThreshold(
  wdi_Xnet,
  powerVector = powers,
  networkType = "signed",
  verbose     = 0
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1))

plot(sft$fitIndices[, 1],
     -sign(sft$fitIndices[, 3]) * sft$fitIndices[, 2],
     xlab = "Soft-threshold power (β)",
     ylab = expression(paste("Scale-free topology fit R"^2)),
     main = "Scale-free fit",
     type = "n", ylim = c(0, 1))
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5)
text(sft$fitIndices[, 1],
     -sign(sft$fitIndices[, 3]) * sft$fitIndices[, 2],
     labels = powers, col = "#1F77B4", cex = 0.9, font = 2)

plot(sft$fitIndices[, 1],
     sft$fitIndices[, 5],
     xlab = "Soft-threshold power (β)",
     ylab = "Mean connectivity",
     main = "Mean connectivity",
     type = "n")
text(sft$fitIndices[, 1],
     sft$fitIndices[, 5],
     labels = powers, col = "#D62728", cex = 0.9, font = 2)

Signed networks need roughly double the power of unsigned ones to reach scale-free topology; we choose β = 10, the lowest power where \(R^2\) reaches 0.8 while mean connectivity is still distinguishable from zero.

3.3 Module detection and dendrogram

SOFT_POWER <- 8L

net <- blockwiseModules(
  wdi_Xnet,
  power             = SOFT_POWER,
  networkType       = "signed",
  TOMType           = "signed",
  minModuleSize     = 10L,
  mergeCutHeight    = 0.25,
  deepSplit         = 2,
  numericLabels     = FALSE,
  pamRespectsDendro = FALSE,
  saveTOMs          = FALSE,
  verbose           = 0
)

table(net$colors)   # grey = unassigned (treated as independent by SF)
plotDendroAndColors(
  net$dendrograms[[1]],
  net$colors[net$blockGenes[[1]]],
  "Module",
  dendroLabels = FALSE,
  hang         = 0.03,
  addGuide     = TRUE,
  guideHang    = 0.05,
  main         = "Indicator dendrogram and module colours"
)
p_dendro <- recordPlot()

3.3.1 Module membership summary

mod_tbl <- as.data.frame(table(Module = net$colors))
mod_tbl$Independent <- mod_tbl$Module == "grey"
mod_tbl <- mod_tbl[order(mod_tbl$Freq, decreasing = TRUE), ]
knitr::kable(mod_tbl, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "WGCNA module sizes (grey = independent pool).")
WGCNA module sizes (grey = independent pool).
Module Freq Independent
turquoise 144 FALSE
blue 109 FALSE
brown 95 FALSE
grey 80 TRUE
yellow 65 FALSE
green 34 FALSE
red 17 FALSE

Grey-labelled indicators are unassigned by WGCNA and treated as the independent pool. On the rank-transformed network this pool is modest — roughly one indicator in seven — with the remaining ~85% falling into a handful of coherent modules (a macro-economic block, a health/mortality block, a demographic block, and so on). It is worth appreciating how much the rank transform buys here: on the raw indicators a Pearson-based network stranded ~80% of features in grey, purely because their monotonic associations do not register as high linear correlations. Rank-transforming before building the network turns the same data into a well-populated module structure without discarding a single indicator.

The grey pool that remains is exactly the regime SF’s split-shadow machinery is designed for: modular indicators are screened within their blocks (controlling for the redundancy inside each bundle), while the independent pool is judged against its own permuted shadows.

3.3.2 Eigengene-based connectivity (kME)

Module eigengenes summarise each module’s profile as a single representative vector. Correlating every indicator with each module eigengene gives its module membership (\(k_{ME}\)) — a continuous measure of how central an indicator is to that module, independent of where the dendrogram was cut.

MEs <- net$MEs
kME <- as.data.frame(signedKME(wdi_Xnet, MEs, outputColumnName = "kME"))

gene_kME <- vapply(seq_along(net$colors), function(i) {
  col <- paste0("kME", net$colors[i])
  if (col %in% colnames(kME)) kME[i, col] else NA_real_
}, numeric(1))

3.3.3 Hub indicators

Intramodular hub indicators are the features most strongly correlated with their module’s eigengene (\(k_{ME}\) near 1) — the ones that best represent their module’s shared variation.

hub_df <- data.frame(
  indicator = colnames(wdi_X),
  label     = wdi_labels[colnames(wdi_X)],
  module    = net$colors,
  kME       = gene_kME,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
hub_df <- hub_df[hub_df$module != "grey" & !is.na(hub_df$kME), ]

top_hubs <- hub_df[order(-hub_df$kME), ][seq_len(min(20L, nrow(hub_df))), ]
top_hubs_disp <- top_hubs[, c("label", "module", "kME")]
knitr::kable(top_hubs_disp, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Top 20 intramodular hub indicators by kME.")

p_hub <- ggplot(top_hubs, aes(x = reorder(label, kME), y = kME, colour = module)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = label, y = 0, yend = kME), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +

                        breaks = unique(top_hubs$module),
                        labels = unique(top_hubs$module)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title    = "Top intramodular hub indicators",
       subtitle = "Ranked by eigengene-based connectivity (kME)",
       x = NULL, y = expression(k[ME])) +
  theme_bw()
p_hub

3.3.4 Final module membership (kME-refined)

Hierarchical clustering can leave borderline indicators mis-assigned at the dendrogram cut. As a final refinement we reassign every indicator to the module whose eigengene it correlates with most strongly (its maximum-kME module). This refined membership — not the raw clustering output — is passed to SF.

module_names <- sub("^kME", "", colnames(kME))
best_module  <- module_names[max.col(as.matrix(kME), ties.method = "first")]

module_membership <- best_module
names(module_membership) <- colnames(wdi_X)

# Recode grey (no strong eigengene correlation) → "independent" so SF
# recognises the independent pool
module_membership[module_membership == "grey"] <- "independent"

membership_xtab <- as.data.frame.matrix(
  table(clustering = net$colors, kME_refined = module_membership))
knitr::kable(membership_xtab,
             caption = "Dendrogram clustering vs kME-refined membership (row = clustering colour).")
Dendrogram clustering vs kME-refined membership (row = clustering colour).
blue brown green independent red turquoise yellow
blue 108 0 0 1 0 0 0
brown 0 91 0 0 0 2 2
green 0 0 34 0 0 0 0
grey 9 7 8 26 8 12 10
red 0 0 0 0 17 0 0
turquoise 0 0 0 0 0 144 0
yellow 2 3 0 0 0 0 60

This module_membership — computed here on all countries — is reused everywhere below: by the single SF run, and by every cross-validation fold and the final refit. WGCNA is unsupervised (built only from indicator–indicator correlations in X, never seeing y), so defining modules on the full matrix does not leak the outcome.

4 Single SF Run

We fit SF once on the full dataset using the module membership derived above and the Python backend, which provides exact TreeSHAP values plus an interaction matrix and is much faster than the pure-R fallback. This requires a Python environment with scikit-learn, shap, and numpy (see ?sf_setup); configure it once per session with sf_setup().

sf_setup()
fit <- sf(
  X = wdi_X,
  y = wdi_y,
  module_membership = module_membership,
  backend = "python",
  verbose = 1L,
  seed = 2026
)

4.1 Stable set

cat("Stable indicators selected:", length(fit$feature_list$feature_name), "\n")
head(sort(fit$stability_freq, decreasing = TRUE), 20)

4.1.1 Domain validation

A stable set is only reassuring if it is the right set. As an annotation-free check, we compare it against the indicators that simply correlate most strongly with life expectancy on their own:

  1. Rank agreement with a naive baseline — do SF’s top features by selection importance line up with the indicators that have the largest absolute Pearson correlation with life expectancy? Agreement means SF is recovering the dominant development signal rather than fitting noise.
  2. Recovery of the strongest univariate signal — of the indicators most correlated with the outcome, how many does the stable set capture?
stable <- fit$feature_list$feature_name

cors <- vapply(wdi_X, function(col) cor(col, wdi_y), numeric(1))

top_imp <- head(fit$final_SHAP$feature_name[order(-fit$final_SHAP$variable_importance)], 15)
top_c   <- names(sort(abs(cors), decreasing = TRUE))[1:15]
cat("Overlap, top-15 SF-importance vs top-15 |cor| indicators:",
    length(intersect(top_imp, top_c)), "/ 15\n")

top_c30 <- names(sort(abs(cors), decreasing = TRUE))[1:30]
cat("Top-30 |cor| indicators recovered in stable set:",
    length(intersect(top_c30, stable)), "/ 30\n")

4.2 Stability plot

plot_stability(fit)

The dashed horizontal line is the tuned pi_thr. The right panel shows the independent pool with its own elbow-detected threshold.

4.3 Feature importance

plot_importance(fit, top_n = 20)

5 Model Comparison: Three-Way Split + Cross-Validated Tuning

5.1 Design

We compare six SF variants formed by two shadow modes × three DML options:

Variant Shadow mode DML
split split none
split_dml split standard
split_mdml split marginal
within within_module none
within_dml within_module standard
within_mdml within_module marginal

We proceed with the following:

  1. Modules from all data. The WGCNA network / module_membership from the section above (built on all countries) is reused throughout.
  2. Vault a test set (~20%) — held out once, scored once, at the very end.
  3. On the remaining ~80% (train): 5-fold CV tunes the hyperparameter grid and compares the six variants on both performance (mean validation-fold \(R^2\)) and stability (Nogueira \(\hat{\Phi}\) of the stable set across folds).
  4. Select one variant by a pre-specified rule (below), refit every variant on the full train set, and report performance on the test set.

Hyperparameters tuned jointly on the validation folds:

Parameter Grid Default
screen_control(drop_fraction) 0.25 (fixed) 0.25
select_control(drop_fraction) 0.05 (fixed) 0.10
select_control(pi_thr) 0.50, 0.60, 0.70 0.60
min_ntree (screen + select) 500 (fixed) 500
n_boots 25 (fixed) 50

3 combinations per variant; within-variant tuning criterion mean validation-fold \(R^2\). All other parameters stay at package defaults.

Selection rule (fixed in advance). For each variant, hyperparameters are tuned by predictive \(R^2\). Variant selection then uses the Nogueira size-corrected stability index \(\hat{\Phi}\): among variants whose \(\hat{\Phi}\) falls within one SE of the maximum, we choose the most parsimonious (smallest mean stable set size \(\bar{k}\)). Predictive performance is reported for reference but does not drive variant selection.

5.2 Setup

library(caret)
VARIANTS <- list(
  split       = list(shadow_mode = "split",         use_dml_residual = FALSE, dml_scope = "indep"),
  split_dml   = list(shadow_mode = "split",         use_dml_residual = TRUE,  dml_scope = "indep"),
  split_mdml  = list(shadow_mode = "split",         use_dml_residual = TRUE,  dml_scope = "all_modules"),
  within      = list(shadow_mode = "within_module", use_dml_residual = FALSE, dml_scope = "indep"),
  within_dml  = list(shadow_mode = "within_module", use_dml_residual = TRUE,  dml_scope = "indep"),
  within_mdml = list(shadow_mode = "within_module", use_dml_residual = TRUE,  dml_scope = "all_modules")
)

GRID <- expand.grid(
  screen_drop = 0.25,
  select_drop = 0.05,
  pi_thr      = c(0.50, 0.60, 0.70),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# ── Three-way split ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Vault ~20% as the held-out test set; the rest is train.
set.seed(2026)
trainval_idx <- as.integer(caret::createDataPartition(
  wdi_y, p = 0.8, list = FALSE))
test_idx     <- setdiff(seq_along(wdi_y), trainval_idx)

X_tv   <- wdi_X[trainval_idx, ]; y_tv   <- wdi_y[trainval_idx]
X_test <- wdi_X[test_idx, ];     y_test <- wdi_y[test_idx]

# Validation role = 5-fold CV *within* train
val_folds <- caret::createFolds(y_tv, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

cat(sprintf("Train: %d  |  Test vault: %d\n", length(y_tv), length(y_test)))

5.3 Fit-and-evaluate helper

fit_eval <- function(X_tr, y_tr, X_te, y_te, variant, grid_row) {

  sc  <- screen_control(
    drop_fraction = grid_row$screen_drop,
    min_ntree     = 500L
  )
  sl  <- select_control(
    drop_fraction    = grid_row$select_drop,
    pi_thr           = grid_row$pi_thr,
    n_boots          = 25L,
    min_ntree        = 500L,
    shadow_mode      = variant$shadow_mode,
    use_dml_residual = variant$use_dml_residual,
    dml_scope        = variant$dml_scope
  )

  fit <- tryCatch(
    sf(X_tr, y_tr,
       module_membership = module_membership,
       screen_params     = sc,
       select_params     = sl,
       backend           = "python",
       seed              = 42L,
       verbose           = 0L),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  stable <- if (!is.null(fit)) fit$feature_list$feature_name else character(0)
  if (length(stable) == 0L)
    return(list(r2 = NA_real_, rmse = NA_real_,
                n_stable = 0L, stable = character(0)))

  rf   <- ranger::ranger(
    y ~ ., num.trees = 300L, seed = 1L,
    data = data.frame(y = y_tr, X_tr[, stable, drop = FALSE])
  )
  pred <- predict(rf, data.frame(X_te[, stable, drop = FALSE]))$predictions

  sse <- sum((pred - y_te)^2)
  sst <- sum((y_te - mean(y_te))^2)

  list(
    r2       = 1 - sse / sst,
    rmse     = sqrt(mean((pred - y_te)^2)),
    n_stable = length(stable),
    stable   = stable
  )
}

5.4 Smoke test

The full tuning sweep is 6 variants × 3 grid rows × 5 validation folds (all sharing the one global module_membership, so no WGCNA re-runs). Before launching, verify that fit_eval() runs end-to-end on a couple of grid rows and a single train/test split.

GRID_smoke <- GRID[1:2, ]
print(GRID_smoke)

set.seed(1)
smoke_split <- caret::createFolds(wdi_y, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)[[1]]
train_idx <- setdiff(seq_along(wdi_y), smoke_split)
test_idx  <- smoke_split

smoke_results <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(GRID_smoke)), function(g) {
  fit_eval(wdi_X[train_idx, ], wdi_y[train_idx],
           wdi_X[test_idx,  ], wdi_y[test_idx],
           VARIANTS[["split"]], GRID_smoke[g, ])
})

data.frame(
  grid_row = seq_len(nrow(GRID_smoke)),
  r2       = vapply(smoke_results, `[[`, numeric(1), "r2"),
  rmse     = vapply(smoke_results, `[[`, numeric(1), "rmse"),
  n_stable = vapply(smoke_results, `[[`, numeric(1), "n_stable")
)

If both rows return a finite r2 and n_stable > 0, fit_eval() and sf() are wired correctly and it is safe to launch the full tune sweep below.

5.5 Cross-validated tuning and stability

For each variant we sweep all 3 grid rows across the five validation folds, record each row’s mean validation \(R^2\), and lock the best-scoring row. At that locked setting we keep the per-fold stable sets, whose Nogueira \(\hat{\Phi}\) is the variant’s stability. Nothing here touches the test vault.

jac_fn <- function(a, b)
  length(intersect(a, b)) / max(length(union(a, b)), 1L)

tune_one <- function(vname) {
  variant <- VARIANTS[[vname]]

  grid_res <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(GRID)), function(g) {
    per_fold <- lapply(seq_along(val_folds), function(fi) {
      vi   <- val_folds[[fi]]
      i_te <- vi; i_tr <- setdiff(seq_along(y_tv), vi)
      r <- fit_eval(X_tv[i_tr, ], y_tv[i_tr],
                    X_tv[i_te, ], y_tv[i_te],
                    variant, GRID[g, ])
      message(sprintf("[%s] g%02d fold%d — r2=%.3f n=%d",
                      vname, g, fi, r$r2, r$n_stable))
      r
    })
    list(
      r2   = mean(vapply(per_fold, `[[`, numeric(1), "r2"), na.rm = TRUE),
      r2s  = vapply(per_fold, `[[`, numeric(1), "r2"),
      sets = lapply(per_fold, `[[`, "stable")
    )
  })

  best_g <- which.max(vapply(grid_res, `[[`, numeric(1), "r2"))
  best   <- grid_res[[best_g]]

  jac <- mean(combn(length(best$sets), 2,
                    function(i) jac_fn(best$sets[[i[1]]], best$sets[[i[2]]]),
                    simplify = TRUE))

  message(sprintf(">>> [%s] DONE — best g%02d cv_r2=%.3f jaccard=%.3f",
                  vname, best_g, best$r2, jac))

  list(
    variant  = vname,
    best_row = GRID[best_g, ],
    cv_r2    = best$r2,
    cv_r2s   = best$r2s,
    jaccard  = jac,
    sets     = best$sets
  )
}

tune <- lapply(names(VARIANTS), tune_one)
names(tune) <- names(VARIANTS)

5.6 Results

5.6.1 Variant selection

For each variant, hyperparameters were tuned by predictive \(R^2\). Variant selection itself uses the Nogueira size-corrected stability index \(\hat{\Phi}\) (Nogueira, Sechidis & Brown, 2018), which corrects the inflation that raw Jaccard exhibits when comparing variants with different stable-set sizes. Among variants whose \(\hat{\Phi}\) falls within one SE of the maximum, we select the most parsimonious (smallest \(\bar{k}\)).

# ── Nogueira Φ̂ helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
.phi_hat <- function(sets, d) {
  M     <- length(sets)
  k_bar <- mean(sapply(sets, length))
  if (k_bar == 0 || k_bar >= d) return(NA_real_)
  pairs <- combn(M, 2, simplify = FALSE)
  sym_d <- sapply(pairs, function(idx) {
    a <- sets[[idx[1]]]; b <- sets[[idx[2]]]
    length(a) + length(b) - 2L * length(intersect(a, b))
  })
  v_obs  <- mean(sym_d) / d
  v_null <- 2 * k_bar * (d - k_bar) / d^2
  1 - v_obs / v_null
}

.phi_se <- function(sets, d) {
  M     <- length(sets)
  k_bar <- mean(sapply(sets, length))
  if (k_bar == 0 || k_bar >= d) return(NA_real_)
  v_null <- 2 * k_bar * (d - k_bar) / d^2
  pairs  <- combn(M, 2, simplify = FALSE)
  v_ij   <- sapply(pairs, function(idx) {
    a <- sets[[idx[1]]]; b <- sets[[idx[2]]]
    (length(a) + length(b) - 2L * length(intersect(a, b))) / d
  })
  sd(v_ij) / (sqrt(length(v_ij)) * v_null)
}

d_total <- ncol(wdi_X)

summary_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tune, function(t) {
  phi    <- .phi_hat(t$sets, d_total)
  phi_se <- .phi_se(t$sets, d_total)
  k_bar  <- mean(sapply(t$sets, length))
  data.frame(
    Variant        = t$variant,
    CV_R2          = round(t$cv_r2, 3),
    CV_R2_SE       = round(sd(t$cv_r2s, na.rm = TRUE) /
                             sqrt(sum(!is.na(t$cv_r2s))), 3),
    Jaccard        = round(t$jaccard, 3),
    Phi            = round(phi, 3),
    Phi_SE         = round(phi_se, 3),
    k_bar          = round(k_bar, 1),
    `Best pi_thr`  = t$best_row$pi_thr,
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
  )
}))

# 1-SE rule on Φ̂; parsimony tiebreaker (smallest k̄)
top     <- which.max(summary_tbl$Phi)
cutoff  <- summary_tbl$Phi[top] - summary_tbl$Phi_SE[top]
in_band <- summary_tbl[summary_tbl$Phi >= cutoff, ]
best_v  <- in_band$Variant[which.min(in_band$k_bar)]

knitr::kable(summary_tbl, align = "lccccccc",
             caption = "Validation-fold performance and Nogueira stability (Φ̂) per variant.")

5.6.2 Pairwise variant comparison

The five validation folds give five paired \(R^2\) values per variant. We test all 15 pairs with a paired Wilcoxon test and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

pairs <- combn(names(VARIANTS), 2, simplify = FALSE)

pw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs, function(p) {
  a <- tune[[p[1]]]$cv_r2s
  b <- tune[[p[2]]]$cv_r2s
  wt <- wilcox.test(a, b, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)
  data.frame(`Method A` = p[1], `Method B` = p[2],
             `ΔR2`      = round(mean(a - b, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
             `p-value`  = round(wt$p.value, 4),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
pw$`p-adj (BH)` <- round(p.adjust(pw$`p-value`, method = "BH"), 4)

5.6.3 Nogueira stability

library(ggplot2)

phi_df <- data.frame(
  Variant = summary_tbl$Variant,
  Phi     = summary_tbl$Phi,
  Phi_SE  = summary_tbl$Phi_SE
)

ggplot(phi_df, aes(x = reorder(Variant, Phi), y = Phi)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1F77B4", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Phi - Phi_SE, ymax = Phi + Phi_SE),
                width = 0.25, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title    = "Nogueira size-corrected stability per variant",
       subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE  |  Dashed line = random-selection null (Φ̂ = 0)",
       x = NULL, y = expression(hat(Phi))) +
  theme_bw()

5.6.4 Final models and held-out test evaluation

We refit every variant on the full train+validation set at its locked hyperparameters, then score each on the vaulted test set — the single time the test data is touched. Each final_models[[v]]$fit is a complete shapleyforest object available for further exploration.

final_models <- lapply(names(VARIANTS), function(vname) {
  variant <- VARIANTS[[vname]]
  row     <- tune[[vname]]$best_row

  sc <- screen_control(
    drop_fraction = row$screen_drop,
    min_ntree     = 500L
  )
  sl <- select_control(
    drop_fraction    = row$select_drop,
    pi_thr           = row$pi_thr,
    n_boots          = 25L,
    min_ntree        = 500L,
    shadow_mode      = variant$shadow_mode,
    use_dml_residual = variant$use_dml_residual,
    dml_scope        = variant$dml_scope
  )

  set.seed(42)
  fit <- sf(X_tv, y_tv,
            module_membership = module_membership,
            screen_params     = sc,
            select_params     = sl,
            backend           = "python",
            seed              = 42L,
            verbose           = 0L)

  stable <- fit$feature_list$feature_name
  rf <- ranger::ranger(
    y ~ ., num.trees = 300L, seed = 1L,
    data = data.frame(y = y_tv, X_tv[, stable, drop = FALSE])
  )
  pred <- predict(rf, data.frame(X_test[, stable, drop = FALSE]))$predictions
  sse  <- sum((pred - y_test)^2); sst <- sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2)

  list(
    fit       = fit,
    test_r2   = 1 - sse / sst,
    test_rmse = sqrt(mean((pred - y_test)^2)),
    n_stable  = length(stable)
  )
})
names(final_models) <- names(VARIANTS)

test_tbl <- data.frame(
  Variant   = names(final_models),
  Test_R2   = round(vapply(final_models, `[[`, numeric(1), "test_r2"),   3),
  Test_RMSE = round(vapply(final_models, `[[`, numeric(1), "test_rmse"), 3),
  n_stable  = vapply(final_models, `[[`, integer(1), "n_stable"),
  Selected  = ifelse(names(final_models) == best_v, "<<", ""),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(test_tbl, align = "lcccc",
             caption = "Held-out test-vault performance (selection made on validation only).")

5.6.5 Top stable indicators by SHAP

The deployed model’s most influential indicators, ranked by mean |SHAP| (average absolute contribution to the life-expectancy prediction across countries), with their WGCNA module and cross-fit selection stability.

best_fit <- final_models[[best_v]]$fit

sh <- best_fit$final_SHAP
sh$score <- if (!is.null(sh$mean_abs_shap)) sh$mean_abs_shap else abs(sh$variable_importance)
sh <- sh[order(-sh$score), ]

shap_tbl <- data.frame(
  Indicator     = unname(wdi_labels[sh$feature_name]),
  Module        = sh$module_membership,
  `Mean |SHAP|` = round(sh$score, 4),
  Stability     = if (!is.null(sh$stability_freq)) round(sh$stability_freq, 3) else NA_real_,
  check.names   = FALSE,
  row.names     = NULL
)[seq_len(min(10L, nrow(sh))), ]

5.6.6 Domain validation

As an annotation-free sanity check: do the indicators SF deems stable line up with the indicators that simply correlate most strongly with life expectancy on their own? If the deployed stable set recovers most of the top univariate hits, SF is capturing the dominant development signal while additionally controlling for the block-correlation structure a plain correlation ignores.

stable_final <- best_fit$feature_list$feature_name

# Recovery of the strongest univariate signal
cors  <- vapply(X_tv, function(col) cor(col, y_tv), numeric(1))
top_c <- names(sort(abs(cors), decreasing = TRUE))[1:30]

domain_tbl <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Selected variant",
             "Deployed stable set size",
             "Top-30 |cor| indicators recovered"),
  Value  = c(best_v,
             as.character(length(stable_final)),
             sprintf("%d / 30", length(intersect(top_c, stable_final)))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
